title: Short Stuff: Wisdom Teeth
summary: Short Stuff episode on wisdom teeth (third molars). Josh and Chuck share personal experiences of having wisdom teeth removed, and discuss the name's origin (Greek phrase for 'teeth of wisdom'), the evolutionary theory that softer modern diets left jaws too small for third molars, and how chewing harder foods promotes jaw bone growth. They cover impacted teeth, which are common, and the argument that wisdom teeth are often removed unnecessarily. They note risks of oral surgery such as nerve and jawbone damage, and suggest a wait-and-see approach with regular dental checkups when teeth are healthy. A University of Saskatchewan anthropologist, Julia Bonner, is cited comparing unnecessary removal to past tonsillectomies. The episode closes with a brief anecdote about anesthesia hallucinations and a tangent about a band name.

segments.title: Opening banter and wisdom teeth introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open by sharing that they had their wisdom teeth removed, and Chuck explains that wisdom teeth are third molars that typically erupt around age seventeen to mid-twenties.

segments.title: Name origin of wisdom teeth
segments.summary: Josh explains the name dates to the Greeks, whose term for wisdom teeth translates roughly to 'teeth of wisdom', because they come in later in life.

segments.title: Why humans have wisdom teeth: diet and jaw size
segments.summary: Chuck says early humans needed wisdom teeth and larger jaws to chew raw, tough foods. Josh questions the timeline of skull changes and the hosts discuss the idea that softer diets left too little room for the teeth, with natural selection lagging behind.

segments.title: Creationist argument about wisdom teeth
segments.summary: Josh describes a creationist argument that uses wisdom teeth as a case where modern diet, not evolution, made the third molar unusable.

segments.title: Impacted teeth and reasons for removal
segments.summary: Chuck explains that many people have one or more wisdom teeth fail to come in, which are called impacted teeth, and that impaction or crowding of other molars is the usual reason for removal. Josh makes a joke about the Simpsons.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Jaw growth from chewing and lack of space
segments.summary: Josh says chewing hard foods promotes jaw bone growth, so a soft Western diet may leave the jaw too small for third molars. Chuck notes that science has not fully explained why impaction happens, and that apes sometimes keep their wisdom teeth.

segments.title: Unnecessary removal and wait-and-see approach
segments.summary: Chuck suggests dentists may push extraction on people who do not need it. Josh says the consensus is to monitor healthy wisdom teeth with regular checkups rather than removing them proactively, and cites University of Saskatchewan evolutionary anthropologist Julia Bonner comparing this to past tonsillectomies.

segments.title: Bone loss and anesthesia hallucination story
segments.summary: Chuck wonders whether keeping his wisdom teeth would have prevented bone loss. He recounts hallucinating a 'Locomotive Lasagna' poster after anesthesia at seventeen, and the hosts joke about a song.

segments.title: Risks of oral surgery
segments.summary: Josh notes that extraction can damage nerves, tissue, and the jawbone, and recounts a story of a surgeon who struggled and sweated during an extraction under local anesthetic, which is why healthy wisdom teeth are often left alone.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes the episode and mentions the show is a production of iHeartRadio.
